description: We are an elite team that combines Earth science expertise with data engineering, geospatial development, and UX design. We build modular software that ingests satellite and model data, applying rigorous statistical tests to determine whether regional trends are truly significant. Through high-performance pipelines and interactive maps, we transform complex Earth observation data into definitive, actionable insights.
summary:
Our web platform, the NASA Earth Observation System // Climate Telemetry & ENSO Observatory, is live at https://schrodingers-cat-nasa.vercel.app/. It includes:

A global Earth view with live hazard and ENSO monitoring (cyclones, seismic activity, El Niño hotspots)
NASA MERRA-2 thermal field and NASA SMAP topsoil moisture maps
An equatorial Pacific sea-surface temperature anomaly view with a year navigator (1980–2050, including the 2023–24 Super El Niño)
An ISS tracker, a city explorer and a °C unit toggle
A downloadable Python script (climate_history.py) that pulls global temperature history from 1800 to the present
The Earth Pulse station comparison, which uses NASA POWER (temperature and weather) and NASA SMAP (soil moisture) for the same coordinates and time period as the station
Cost
	Estimated cost
Lean version	about 170–280 AED
Full version (with CO₂ and GPS)	about 300–550 AED
Website hosting and NASA data	free
Impact

Because the station is cheap, it can be built in many places. That could mean more ground-truth measurements to validate satellite data, hands-on climate learning for students, and early flags of unusual local changes such as heat spikes or soil drying.

Future Work
Deploy multiple stations and build a network of ground points
Add the optional solar, UV, CO₂ and GPS modules
Field-test the enclosure in UAE heat and rain
Add automated statistical comparison between ground and satellite data
details:
The Problem

Satellites give us a global view of climate and environmental change, but those changes happen locally. A single satellite pixel can cover a large area, so it is hard to verify at small scale whether what the satellite sees matches what is happening on the ground.

Our Solution

Earth Pulse Field Station is a low-cost, outdoor sensor station that measures conditions on site and flags unusual changes. Our website then compares the station’s data with NASA data for the same coordinates and time period. This gives communities, schools and researchers an affordable way to check satellite data against real ground conditions.

How It Works

  1. Sense: Sensors measure temperature, humidity, air pressure and soil moisture.
  2. Detect: An ESP32 microcontroller measures every few minutes, learns what is normal for that location, builds a baseline, and flags readings that drift far from it.
  3. Transmit: Data is sent over Wi-Fi to our website.
  4. Compare: The website places ground data next to NASA data in side-by-side charts, so users can see whether ground and satellite agree.

An alert LED on the station and a flag on the website show when a reading is unusual.

Hardware

  • ESP32 microcontroller with Wi-Fi
  • BME280 sensor (temperature, humidity, pressure)
  • Capacitive soil moisture sensor
  • Rechargeable battery with charging board
  • Optional upgrades: solar panel, UV sensor, CO₂ sensor, GPS

3D-Printed Enclosure

We designed a custom housing in Plasticity (140 × 98 × 42.5 mm) with:

  • Bays for the battery, ESP32 and charger, with 0.4 mm clearance
  • Four M2 screw posts for the BME280
  • A gasket groove in the lid for a rain seal
  • White PETG or ASA to cope with UAE heat
